# Approximation of sound with Fourier series

 
 

## Introduction
One can think of sound as something composed of *pure tones* - the sound you get from pressing a key on the piano. 
It turns out that pure tones can be represented in terms of trigonometric functions, a fact that we will now verify. Let us take a look at the sinusoid
$x_1(t)=\sin(2\pi ft)$. This represents a sound signal with $f$ oscillations per second (or frequency $f$). 
Quick oscillations give light tones, while slow oscillations give dark tones. 
The computer represents sound as values in the interval $[-1,1]$: Small numbers give weak sounds, while big numbers give loud sounds. 
If we want to listen to the sound signal $x$ on a computer, we need to specify how often the sound should be sampled. 
This is called the *sampling rate*, $f_s$, and is measured in *samples per second*.
In the following we will choose $f_s=44100$. We will also restrict to sound durations of \texttt{numsec} seconds:
```{python}
import numpy as np

f_s = 44100
numsec=3
t = np.linspace(0, numsec, f_s*numsec).reshape((-1,1))
```
Here we also made a list of all the time values. The sound $x$ can then be generated as follows.
```{python}
f = 440
x_1 = np.sin(2*np.pi*f*t)
```
In this project we will use the following function
which creates a \texttt{wav}-file from the sound samples \texttt{x} with the given sampling rate 
```{python}
import math, wave, sys, os, subprocess
from numpy import *

max_amplitude = 2**15-1 # iinfo('int16').max if numpy >= 1.0.3

def audiowrite(filename, x, fs):
    ofile = wave.open(filename, 'w')
    ofile.setsampwidth(2)
    ofile.setframerate(fs)
    ofile.setnchannels(1)
    x=max_amplitude*x
    x=x.astype(int16)
    x=x.astype(uint16)
    ofile.writeframesraw(x.astype(uint16).tostring())
    ofile.close()
```    
The array data type can be arbitrary as it is converted to numpy.uint16 in this function.
After invoking this you can play the resulting \texttt{wav}-file using any program on your computer. If you do this you should hear something similar to that of a piano key. 
If you exchange the code above with
```{python}
f_1=440
f_2=880
x_2 = 0.5*np.sin(2*np.pi*f_1*t) + 0.5*np.sin(2*np.pi*f_2*t)
```
you should be able to recognise the combination of two pure tones, one of them being the one you already have listened to. 
By multiplying each sinusoid with $0.5$ we ensure that the sound samples never exceed $1$. 

The idea is that more general sound may also be represented, or at least approximated well, in terms of pure tones. Let us dive deeper into this, 
to see if it is the case that many sounds can indeed be decomposed with pure tones as building blocks. 
We will look at two possible approximations of sound. Both will be in terms of the spaces
$$
\begin{aligned} 
V_{N,T}=\text{Span}\{ 1, & \cos(2\pi t/T),\cos(2\pi 2t/T,...,\cos(2\pi Nt/T), \\
                                        & \sin(2\pi t/T),\sin(2\pi 2t/T,...,\sin(2\pi Nt/T)\}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-basisfunctions}
The functions in $V_{N,T}$ are defined on $[0,T]$. 
The sounds we will look at will be assumed to have period $T$, and the functions listed above satisfy this.
From left to right the functions above have frequencies $0,1/T,2/T,...,n/T$. 

## Approximating sound with the method of least squares
Our first way of approximation will be as least squares approximations in terms of the inner product
$$\langle f,g \rangle = \int_0^T f(t)g(t)\,dt$$ {#eq-innerproddef}

::: {#exr-1}
Show that the functions listed in @eq-basisfunctions are orthogonal w.r.t. the inner product given by @eq-innerproddef.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="sols"}
*Solution*: For $m\neq n$ we have that
\begin{align*}
\lefteqn{\langle \cos(2\pi mt/T),\cos(2\pi nt/T) \rangle} \\
&= \int_0^T \cos(2\pi mt/T)\cos(2\pi nt/T)\,dt \\
&= \frac{1}{2}\int_0^T \left( \cos(2\pi (m+n)t/T) + \cos(2\pi (m-n)t/T) \right)\,dt \\
&= \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{T}{2\pi(m+n)} \sin(2\pi (m+n)t/T) + \frac{T}{2\pi(m-n)}\sin(2\pi (m-n)t/T)\right]_0^T \\
&= 0.
\end{align*}
here we used the trigonometric identities $\cos(x\pm y)=\cos x\cos y\mp \sin x\sin y$, and that the trigonometric functions have period $2\pi$.
The other orthogonality relations follow in the same way.
:::
:::

We also get that 
\begin{align*}
\lefteqn{\langle \cos(2\pi nt/T),\cos(2\pi nt/T) \rangle} \\
&= \int_0^T \cos^2(2\pi nt/T)\,dt = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^T (\cos(4\pi nt/T) + 1)\,dt = \frac{T}{2},
\end{align*}
and similarly $\langle \sin(2\pi nt/T),\sin(2\pi nt/T) \rangle=\frac{T}{2}$, and $\langle 1,1\rangle=T$.
From this it follows that the best approximation of $f$ from $V_{N,T}$ is 
$$
a_0 + \sum_{n=1}^N \left( a_n\cos(2\pi nt/T) + b_n\sin(2\pi nt/T) \right),
$$
where 
\begin{align*}
a_0&=\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T f(t)\,dt \\
a_n&=\frac{2}{T}\int_0^T f(t)\cos(2\pi nt/T)\,dt \\
b_n&=\frac{2}{T}\int_0^T f(t)\sin(2\pi nt/T)\,dt
\end{align*}
We define the square wave with period by $T$ as
$$
x_s(t)=\begin{cases} 1 & \text{ for } 0\leq t<T/2 \\ -1 & \text{ for } T/2\leq t<T.\end{cases}
$$

::: {#exr-2}
Compute the samples of the square wave for three seconds, and listen to it.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="sols"}
*Solution*: The following code can be used to generate the sound.
```{python}
sphalf = int(f_s/(2*f))
oneperiod = np.block( [np.ones(sphalf),-np.ones(sphalf)])
x_3 = np.tile(oneperiod, numsec*f)
```
:::
:::

::: {#exr-3}
Find the best approximation of $x_s(T)$ from $V_{N,T}$.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="sols"}
*Solution*: We get
\begin{align*}
a_0&=\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T f(t)\,dt = \frac{1}{T}\int_0^{T/2} dt - \frac{1}{T}\int_{T/2}^T dt = 1/2-1/2=0\\
a_n&=\frac{2}{T}\int_0^T f(t)\cos(2\pi nt/T)\,dt \\
      &= \frac{2}{T}\left(\int_0^{T/2} \cos(2\pi nt/T)\,dt - \frac{2}{T}\int_{T/2}^T \cos(2\pi nt/T)\,dt \right)\\
      &= \frac{1}{\pi n}\left(  \left[ \sin(2\pi nt/T) \right]_0^{T/2} - \left[ \sin(2\pi nt/T) \right]_{T/2}^T\right) =0
\end{align*}
where we used that $\sin(k\pi)=0$ for all integers $k$. We also get
\begin{align*}
b_n&=\frac{2}{T}\int_0^T f(t)\sin(2\pi nt/T)\,dt \\
      &= \frac{2}{T}\left(\int_0^{T/2} \sin(2\pi nt/T)\,dt - \frac{2}{T}\int_{T/2}^T \sin(2\pi nt/T)\,dt \right)\\
      &= \frac{1}{\pi n}\left(  \left[ -\cos(2\pi nt/T) \right]_0^{T/2} + \left[ \cos(2\pi nt/T) \right]_{T/2}^T\right) \\
      &= \frac{1}{\pi n}(2-2\cos(\pi n)) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{ for } n \text{ even} \\ 4/(\pi n) & \text{ for } n \text{ odd}\end{cases}
\end{align*}
When $N$ is odd the best approximation is 
$$\frac{4}{\pi} \sin(2\pi t/T) + \frac{4}{3\pi} \sin(2\pi 3t/T) + \frac{4}{5\pi}\sin(2\pi 5t/T) + \cdots + \frac{4}{N\pi}\sin(2\pi Nt/T).$$
:::
:::

Once $N$ has been set, the vector $(a_0,a_1,...,a_N,b_1,...,b_N)$ can be found with the following code
```{python}
#| eval: false
coeffs = np.zeros((2*N+1))
coeffs[(N+1)::2] = 4/(np.arange(1, N+1, 2)*np.pi)
```


Let us now see how we can plot a general Fourier series
$$
a_0 + \sum_{n=1}^N \left( a_n\cos(2\pi nt/T) + b_n\sin(2\pi nt/T) \right),
$$
which can be written as 
$$
\begin{pmatrix} 
1 & \cos\left(\frac{2\pi 1\cdot t}{T}\right) & \cdots & \cos\left(\frac{2\pi Nt}{T}\right) & \sin\left(\frac{2\pi 1t}{T}\right) & \cdots & \sin\left(\frac{2\pi Nt}{T}\right)
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} a_0 \\ a_1 \\ \vdots \\ a_N \\ b_1 \\ \vdots \\ b_N \end{pmatrix}
$$
Here $\mathbf{t}=(t_1,t_2,...,t_s)$ is a vector, so we need to compute
$$
\begin{pmatrix} 
1 & \cos\left(\frac{2\pi 1t_1}{T}\right) & \cdots & \cos\left(\frac{2\pi Nt_1}{T}\right) & \sin\left(\frac{2\pi 1t_1}{T}\right) & \cdots & \sin\left(\frac{2\pi Nt_1}{T}\right) \\
1 & \cos\left(\frac{2\pi 1t_2}{T}\right) & \cdots & \cos\left(\frac{2\pi Nt_2}{T}\right) & \sin\left(\frac{2\pi 1t_2}{T}\right) & \cdots & \sin\left(\frac{2\pi Nt_2}{T}\right) \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
1 & \cos\left(\frac{2\pi 1t_s}{T}\right) & \cdots & \cos\left(\frac{2\pi Nt_s}{T}\right) & \sin\left(\frac{2\pi 1t_s}{T}\right) & \cdots & \sin\left(\frac{2\pi Nt_s}{T}\right)
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} a_0 \\ a_1 \\ \vdots \\ a_N \\ b_1 \\ \vdots \\ b_N \end{pmatrix}
$$
If we define the column vector $\mathbf{v}=(1,2,...,N)$, the matrix above can be written as
$$\begin{pmatrix} 1_s & \cos(2\pi\mathbf{t}\mathbf{v}^T/T) & \sin(2\pi\mathbf{t}\mathbf{v}^T/T) \end{pmatrix},$$ {#eq-usethisexpr}
where $\sin$ and $\cos$ operate elementwise on the matrix. This means that the samples of the Fourier series can be found with the following function.
```{python}
def compute_fourier(t, coeffs):
    K = np.shape(coeffs)[0]; N = int((K-1)/2); s = np.shape(t)[0];
    v = np.arange(1,N+1).reshape((1,-1))
    A = np.block( [ np.ones((s,1)), np.cos(2*np.pi*t@v/T), np.sin(2*np.pi*t@v/T) ] )
    return A@coeffs
```









::: {#exr-4}
Plot the Fourier series of the square wave for $N=3,7,11$, together with the square wave itself. Plot over $[0,T]$. 

::: {.content-visible when-meta="sols"}
*Solution*: The following code can be used.
```{python}
#| label: fig-fourier1
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

T=1/f; npp=100;
tp = np.linspace(0,T,npp).reshape((-1,1))

for N in [3,7,11]:
    coeffs = np.zeros((2*N+1))
    coeffs[(N+1)::2] = 4/(np.arange(1, N+1, 2)*np.pi)
    x = compute_fourier(tp, coeffs)
    plt.plot(tp,x)  
x = (np.logical_and(tp>=0, tp<T/2)).astype(float) - (np.logical_and(tp>=T/2, tp<T)).astype(float)
plt.plot(tp,x)
plt.legend(['N=3','N=7','N=11','Square wave'])
plt.show()
```
:::
:::

## Approximating sound using interpolation
The second way of approximating a sound $x$ is by finding a unique function in $V_{N,T}$ that interpolates $x$ at a given set of points.
If $t$ is one of the interpolation points we must have that
$$
a_0 + \sum_{n=1}^N \left( a_n\cos(2\pi nt/T) + b_n\sin(2\pi nt/T) \right) = f(t),
$$
which can be written as 
$$
\begin{pmatrix} 
1 & \cos\left(\frac{2\pi 1\cdot t}{T}\right) & \cdots & \cos\left(\frac{2\pi Nt}{T}\right) & \sin\left(\frac{2\pi 1t}{T}\right) & \cdots & \sin\left(\frac{2\pi Nt}{T}\right)
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} a_0 \\ a_1 \\ \vdots \\ a_N \\ b_1 \\ \vdots \\ b_N \end{pmatrix}
=
f(t)
$$
Since there are $2N+1$ unknowns $a_i,b_i$, one would guess that we need $2N+1$ equations, i.e., $2N+1$ interpolation points. 
We will choose these as $Tk/(2N+1)$ for $0\leq k\leq 2N$, i.e., uniformly distributed over one period. 
With $K=2N+1$, since  the samples of the square wave is 
$$x_s(Tk/(2N+1))=\begin{cases} 1 & \text{ for } k=0,...,N\\ -1 & \text{ for } k =N+1,...,2N\end{cases}$$
and since $2\pi (Tk/(2N+1))/T=2\pi k/(2N+1)$, this gives the following equations.
$$
\begin{pmatrix} 
1 & \cos\left(\frac{2\pi 1\cdot 0}{K}\right) & \cdots & \cos\left(\frac{2\pi N\cdot 0}{K}\right) & \sin\left(\frac{2\pi 1\cdot 0}{K}\right) & \cdots & \sin\left(\frac{2\pi N\cdot 0}{K}\right) \\
1 & \cos\left(\frac{2\pi 1\cdot 1}{K}\right) & \cdots & \cos\left(\frac{2\pi N\cdot 1}{K}\right) & \sin\left(\frac{2\pi 1\cdot 1}{K}\right) & \cdots & \sin\left(\frac{2\pi N\cdot 1}{K}\right) \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
1 & \cos\left(\frac{2\pi 1\cdot 2N}{K}\right) & \cdots & \cos\left(\frac{2\pi N\cdot 2N}{K}\right) & \sin\left(\frac{2\pi 1\cdot 2N}{K}\right) & \cdots & \sin\left(\frac{2\pi N\cdot 2N}{K}\right)
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} a_0 \\ a_1 \\ \vdots \\ a_N \\ b_1 \\ \vdots \\ b_N \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ \vdots \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ \vdots \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}
$$
It turns out that the matrix here is invertible (but we will not prove this). Also, this system can be solved much more efficiently when expressed in a different way. 

Note that, if we define the column vectors $\mathbf{t}=(0,1,...,K-1)$, $\mathbf{v}=(1,2,...,N)$, @eq-usethisexpr now takes the form
$$
\begin{pmatrix} 1_K & \cos(2\pi\mathbf{t}\mathbf{v}^T/K) & \sin(2\pi\mathbf{t}\mathbf{v}^T/K) \end{pmatrix},
$$
where $\sin$ and $\cos$ operate elementwise on the matrix. This means that the following code finds the coefficients $a_i,b_i$:
```{python}
N = 10; K = 2*N+1;
tpp = np.arange(0,K).reshape((-1,1))
v = np.arange(1,N+1).reshape((1,-1))
A=np.block( [ np.ones((K,1)), np.cos(2*np.pi*tpp@v/K), np.sin(2*np.pi*tpp@v/K) ] )
oneperiod = np.block( [np.ones(N+1),-np.ones(N)] )
coeffs=np.linalg.solve(A,oneperiod)
```

::: {#exr-7}
Plot the Fourier series where $a_i,b_i$ are obtained as above, together with the square wave. 

::: {.content-visible when-meta="sols"}
*Solution*: Once \texttt{coeffs} has been found as above, the Fourier series can be plotted as follows.
```{python}
#| label: fig-fourier2
x = compute_fourier(tp, coeffs)
plt.plot(tp,x)  
x = (np.logical_and(tp>=0, tp<T/2)).astype(float) - (np.logical_and(tp>=T/2, tp<T)).astype(float)
plt.plot(tp,x)
plt.legend(['N=10','Square wave'])
```
:::
:::
